title: cross-region-failover-streaming-cost-sweep-may-2026
content:
Summary:

This note captures an exploratory sweep measuring the incremental latency and token-cost overhead when active streaming sessions fail over across regions. Motivation came from a customer report where a small percentage of streaming responses showed 3–6s tail spikes during regional failover windows. We tried to reproduce in a controlled lab and characterize mechanisms that contribute to the observed spikes: TCP/TLS connection reestablishment, stream resume behavior (gRPC vs HTTP/2 vs QUIC), client-side flush/retry patterns, DNS TTL behavior, and routing-level redirection from the edge.

Key findings (high level):
- Cross-region failover causes a mix of quick reconnects (~100–500ms) and long tail events (1.5–6s). Long tails occur when both (a) client waits for TCP/TLS timeout and (b) the application-layer resume requires re-warming KV-cache/decoder state.
- gRPC bidi streaming shows the most deterministic reconnect cost because many clients immediately open a new channel; however, server-side session reattachment cost (KV cache miss) adds ~30–120ms per warmup token and can amplify latency by ~200–800ms for short responses.
- HTTP/2 streaming (chunked responses) tends to hide some reconnect cost via chunk buffering on intermediaries, but when upstream changes region, the proxy buffer drops and client designers that wait for the final chunk can see >1s stalls.
- QUIC (simulated via experimental client) reduced reconnect times for handshake (~40–150ms) and avoided TCP slow start, but not all edge stacks support QUIC routing for idle sessions. Where QUIC was fully end-to-end, median reconnect time was ~120ms vs ~320ms for TLS-over-TCP.
- DNS TTL and edge control-plane reconfiguration can add 200–1200ms delay in certain realworld cloud setups (observed in our GCP testbed when failover triggered route propagation).

Experiment setup:
- Date: 2026-05-15 to 2026-05-18
- Hardware: Dedicated test cluster with 2 r5.large clients, 3 redwood-inference serving nodes (p4d-equivalent) across two regions (us-west1, us-east1). All nodes in separate AZs.
- Network: Emulated cross-region link with baseline RTT 70ms, 90ms, and high-variance case up to 150ms RTT and 2% p50 packet loss for stress runs (tc/netem).
- Workload: 10k streaming requests total per run, each request generates 32 tokens on average; mix of small (8 token), medium (32 token), long (128 token). Inter-arrival: Poisson with mean 150ms.
- Protocols tested: gRPC bidi-streaming (channel-per-request), HTTP/2 chunked-response (single request), QUIC-based datagram streaming (experimental client).
- Failover trigger: Controlled cut of us-west1 cluster and re-route of traffic to us-east1. Two failover modes: (A) instant cut (simulate AZ/region outage), (B) graceful shift (edge reconfig with 5s drain window).
- Metrics: per-request p50/p95/p99 latency to first token and final token, reconnect time (time between last server token and first reconnected token), per-token CPU cost on server, cache-hit fraction for KV prefix cache.

Observations (data highlights):
- Instant cut (mode A):
  - gRPC: p50 reconnect 180ms, p95 430ms, p99 2.1s. Final-token p99 spikes up to 3.8s for short responses that rely on a final flush.
  - HTTP/2: p50 reconnect 240ms, p95 560ms, p99 2.6s. Observed extra tail when intermediate proxy held partially-sent frames that were dropped.
  - QUIC: p50 reconnect 95ms, p95 200ms, p99 700ms (but only when route was QUIC-compatible end-to-end).

- Graceful shift (mode B):
  - When edge reconfig provided explicit 5s drain, the majority of sessions completed without reconnect. However, ~12% of sessions that attempted mid-response reconnects due to packet loss still needed reattaching leading to p99 1.2s.

- KV-cache warming:
  - For gRPC streams that reconnected to a different serving node, the KV prefix cache hit rate fell from 97% to 12% immediately after failover. Warmup recovered to 90% after ~8k tokens generated on the new node. The initial cold path added ~60–150ms of CPU and memory-locality cost per token for the first ~8 tokens, magnifying for short responses.

- Client flush semantics:
  - Clients that waited for a final chunk (common HTTP-style clients) saw bigger tails than clients that consume incremental tokens. Recommend client-side streaming consumer loops rather than 'wait-for-final'.

- DNS and edge control plane events:
  - In some runs the redirect from edge took an extra 200–1200ms because of DNS caching at clients and intermediate resolvers. Tests with DNS TTL=60s replicated slower convergence; TTL=5s reduced that window but increased resolver query load.

Synthetic breakdown (typical long-tail case ~2.4s):
  - 800ms: DNS/edge propagation + resolver retries
  - 300ms: TCP/TLS handshake (multiple RTTs depending on congestion control)
  - 600ms: application-level reattachment + KV-cache cold path warmup
  - 700ms: client-side backoff + message re-send handling

Recommendations (short-term):
1) Client consumer guidance: update SDKs to document "incremental consumption" as best practice (do not wait for final chunk). Add example for both gRPC and HTTP streaming.
2) Server: implement lightweight session resume token that preserves minimal decoder/KV state across nodes so reconnecting clients can restore a compact session without full decoder warmup. Prototype attempt in PR#1873.
3) Edge: coordinate lower DNS TTL for active failover customers while providing query-rate protection. Consider signaling via ephemeral routing header to speed up edge hand-off.
4) QUIC pilot: enable QUIC routing for a small percentage of traffic and track end-to-end support. QUIC consistently reduced handshake latency in our lab.
5) Instrumentation: add a "session-reattach" metric and probe that records where warmup happened (which node served token-0). Use this to quantify cross-node migration.
6) Backoff defaults: reduce client-side retry backoff ceiling for streaming reconnects (default 2s -> 500ms) in SDKs to avoid compounding user-observed tail.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Real cloud control planes differ: we saw different propagation delays on AWS vs GCP in separate ad-hoc runs. Need wider cross-cloud sweep before generalizing DNS TTL guidance.
- Security implications of session resume token: how to avoid leaking state across tenant boundaries; needs design review with security team.
- How much state is safe to carry in a minimal resume token vs the complexity of implementation in the runtime?

Next steps / short plan:
- (Immediate) Add incremental-consumption guidance and example snippets to node/python SDKs (owner: Maya, ETA: 2026-05-28).
- (Prototype) Finish minimal session-resume prototype in serving-runtime; run canary with internal traffic (owner: Ravi, ETA: 2026-06-11).
- (Measure) Quic pilot with 5% traffic and cross-cloud evaluation (owner: Claire, ETA: 2026-06-20).
- (Investigate) Run cross-cloud DNS/edge sweep (AWS/GCP/Azure) to quantify control-plane propagation (owner: infra-team, ETA: 2026-06-30).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally exploratory; numbers are from lab emulations and small-scale canary runs. Expect variation in production.
- Attached artifacts: a small Jupyter notebook (linked in PR) with raw traces and analysis scripts. The notebook includes a reproducible tc/netem configuration for the testbed.

Rough playback log (details for triage):
- 2026-05-15: initial replicates in lab; discovered DNS TTL effect.
- 2026-05-16: KV-cache impact measured; found 8k-token warmup knee.
- 2026-05-17: QUIC client added; observed consistent handshake improvements.
- 2026-05-18: consolidated runs and produced this note.

If this is useful to product or CS for customer-facing guidance I can draft a short one-pager for the KB. Otherwise, next iteration will focus on the session-resume prototype and a more systematic cross-cloud comparison.

-- Claire
